prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: Having read the whole first-round exchange, I keep my configuration unchanged: one prize part, B042, to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. All six of us arrived at the same trio, but the reason to stay with it is the science. Incretin physiology in humans (Holst), identification and synthesis of the insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) peptide (Mojsov), and GLP-1 and GLP-2 receptor biology and translation (Drucker) form one coherent physiological arc, and that arc is what independent randomized outcome trials in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal disease have since validated. It is mature, original and clearly delimited, and it explains why the drugs work. I do not see a second part that adds enough to justify splitting it: any second part would force the GLP-1 credit below three names or add a fourth person, and no second candidate has a cleaner attribution than B042 has after the third name is settled.
statement.case_against: The case against remains attribution and wording, not merit. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide relative to Habener and colleagues cannot be verified from the material supplied to us, and I am working from recollection of that history. Habener sits outside the three-name cap, and so does Knudsen, whose design of liraglutide and semaglutide delivered the therapy at scale. A citation confined to physiology can be read as under-crediting the engineering; a citation that names the agonists risks a prize for a drug class. If the committee concludes that Mojsov's contribution cannot be separated from Habener's group in a way we can defend in writing, I would move to Knudsen as the third name, because a clean attribution to a contribution nobody disputes is better than a disputed one. That is a fallback, not my current position.

responses.point: Linnarsson moved from a Knudsen-inclusive trio at opening to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, but states that if the therapeutic step is the heart of the achievement then Knudsen should replace Mojsov.
responses.response: I agree with your revised trio and with your stated fallback, which matches mine. Where I would hold the line is on what the prize is for: the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is what made rational agonist design possible, so it sits upstream of Knudsen's work in the logic of discovery. I would not accept the argument that the drugs are the heart of the achievement, because a prize for the drugs would have to name the agonist developers and would no longer be a physiology prize. I would switch only on a priority finding, not on the weight given to engineering.

responses.point: The chair would keep the citation on physiology so as not to assert a priority that cannot be adjudicated, and asks whether the committee can state what Mojsov and Habener each contributed on proglucagon peptides and the active form.
responses.response: I accept the chair's drafting approach and have kept the citation to physiology and the active form. My answer to the first question is limited: as I recall it, Habener's group has a strong claim on proglucagon cloning and sequence, while Mojsov's contribution is the identification and synthesis of the truncated, insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) form. These are different steps, which is why the wording 'identification of its active form' is more defensible than a general priority claim. I cannot verify the detail and the committee should not treat my recollection as a finding. If we cannot be comfortable with it, the third place goes to Knudsen, not to a two-name prize.

responses.point: El-Manira asks that the tool-versus-discovery question be answered once and applied consistently to B004 and B029, and describes the B042 citation as one that keeps the prize on discovery rather than a product.
responses.response: I agree on the citation and I think your consistency request is fair. My rule would be that a tool can qualify if the discovery it enabled, or the tool itself, is original and widely transformative, but that it also has to survive the attribution test. B004 and B029 both fail that test this year for different reasons: B029 has six names that cannot be cut to three without excluding Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenboeck, and B004 has a similar problem across the sequencing chemistry and the commercial platform. That is a reason to leave both for a later year rather than a verdict that tools can never be recognised.

responses.point: Sandberg-Rickard notes that a topic this widely known risks being treated as the default and receiving less scrutiny than lower-ranked candidates, and asks what the single Nobel-level discovery is behind B041.
responses.response: I agree that unanimity should not replace scrutiny, and that is why I tested B042 against its own weakest point, attribution, and kept a named fallback. On B041, I rank it as an alternative but share your question: the clear originating discovery is hard to separate from the clinical demonstration and antibody engineering, so I would not put it forward as a second prize part this year. Because B041 is close to my own field, I am being cautious and would not push it beyond the alternatives list.

responses.point: Perlmann raises whether a two-part prize pairing the incretin discovery with a second achievement would be better than a single-part prize, given how far ahead B042 is.
responses.response: I have considered it and I still favour a single part. The strength of B042 is that the three names cover one continuous achievement. Adding B038, B013 or B015 would not strengthen B042, and each of those carries its own attribution gap (Eshhar for CAR-T, Zhou for HPV, the Biogen team and Hua for B015). Being far ahead in opening support is not a reason to add a second part to the prize. If the committee wants one, I would look to B038 as the most developed alternative, but only if the Rosenberg question is settled and I do not see that settled yet.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide can be defended in writing against Habener and colleagues; I rely on recollection and have not checked the primary record.
Whether the committee will accept a physiology-only citation as fair to Knudsen's engineering of liraglutide and semaglutide, or will insist the third name reflect it.
Whether a second part is worth considering at all, and if so whether Eshhar's omission and the Rosenberg question make B038 weaker than I currently judge.
How consistently the committee applies its tool-versus-discovery rule across B004 and B029.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. No documented personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted candidate. B041 (anti-TNF therapy in rheumatoid arthritis) is close to my field of experimental rheumatology, and I have no documented tie to Feldmann or Maini; I have kept it only as an alternative and flag the proximity so colleagues can weigh it.
